Its elements are exactly the ordered pairs $(a,b)$
This maximal atlas is the **product smooth structure** of $M\times N$.
A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that
The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when
The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.
The local Riemannian volume densities glue to a positive smooth density independent of coordinates.
For physical unit assignments use length coordinates $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ and spatial coordinates in metres
when a global stationary potential is actually defined, $\Phi_\xi:=-cA_a\xi^a$ has volts and $q\Phi_\xi$ has joules.
Define the lapse $N_\xi:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and unit observer $u_\xi:=\xi/N_\xi$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $M=\mathbb R\times\Sigma$ is the Cartesian product equipped with the smooth product structure of [F3], hence is a smooth four-manifold. The tensor $g=-N^2 dx^0\otimes dx^0+h$ is smooth and symmetric. At each $(x^0,y)$ the tangent space splits as $\mathbb R\partial_{x^0}\oplus T_y\Sigma$, and for $a\in\mathbb R$ and $v\in T_y\Sigma$ its quadratic form is $-N(y)^2a^2+h_y(v,v)$. Since $N(y)>0$ and $h_y$ is positive definite by [F4], this form has one negative direction and three positive directions, and its direct-sum matrix is nondegenerate; hence it has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ by [F5].

The field $\partial_{x^0}$ is smooth and has squared norm $-N^2<0$, so it is future timelike for the selected time orientation. Its local flow translates $x^0$ and fixes $y\in\Sigma$; since $N$ and $h$ are independent of $x^0$, this flow pulls $g$ back to itself and hence $\mathcal L_{\partial_{x^0}}g=0$ by [F6]. Thus the field is Killing, and its lapse equals the prescribed $N$ by [F10].

By [F7], $dV_h$ is a globally defined positive smooth density, so the integral measure does not depend on an orientation or chart. Each point has a coordinate ball whose closure is compact inside a chart; compactness supplies a finite subcover by such balls. On each closure the smooth density coefficient is bounded and the coordinate ball has finite Euclidean volume, so $dV_h(\Sigma)<\infty$. The profiles $T=T_0/N$ and $\mu=(\mu_0-q\Phi)/N$ are smooth because $N$ is smooth and strictly positive. Their length-coordinate conventions follow from [F8], while $q\Phi$ has energy units by [F9]. This establishes that all prescribed data and the volume density used by the hydrostatic functional are well defined.

derivations.claim: Choose a closed interval $I_0\subset U$ whose interior contains $\mu_0$, and for $r\in I_0$ define $f(r,x)=N(x)p(T_0/N(x),(r-q\Phi(x))/N(x))/(k_BT_0)$. The image of $I_0\times\Sigma$ in $D$ is compact, so $p_\mu$ and $p_{\mu\mu}$ are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Since $N$ is continuous and positive on compact $\Sigma$, its image has a minimum $N_{\min}>0$; also $dV_h(\Sigma)<\infty$. The one-variable mean value theorem and uniform continuity of $\partial_r f$ make the difference quotients of $f$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $\partial_r f=p_\mu(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(k_BT_0)$. For these quotients $q_h$, the estimate $|\int_\Sigma q_h\,dV_h-\int_\Sigma\partial_r f\,dV_h|\le dV_h(\Sigma)\sup_x|q_h(x)-\partial_r f(r,x)|$ tends to zero. Thus differentiation passes through the finite-volume integral and yields $\partial_{\mu_0}W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_\mu/(k_BT_0)\,dV_h$.

Applying the same uniform difference-quotient argument to $\partial_r f$, whose derivative is $\partial_r^2 f=p_{\mu\mu}(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(N k_BT_0)$, gives $\partial_{\mu_0}^2W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_{\mu\mu}/(N k_BT_0)\,dV_h$. The factors $N$ cancel once in the first derivative, while the second derivative retains the positive factor $1/N$.

By [A1], each integrand value in the second formula is nonnegative because $N(x)>0$, $k_B>0$, and $T_0>0$. By [F3], the Riemannian volume density is positive, so its integral is nonnegative and therefore $\chi_{\rm hs}\ge0$.
